content: The BCG vaccine (live) should not be administered concurrently with antibiotics due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. It is contraindicated, and administration of live bacterial vaccines should be delayed until antibiotic therapy is completed. Close monitoring is required when penicillin G aqueous is used, as it can reduce the effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors like camrelizumab, cemiplimab, cosibelimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab through unspecified interaction mechanisms. Coadministration may interfere with the therapeutic effects of these inhibitors, necessitating caution and close monitoring. Penicillin G aqueous can interact with other drugs through various mechanisms. For example, chloramphenicol decreases its effects via pharmacodynamic antagonism, while chlorothiazide and hydrochlorothiazide increase its levels by reducing renal clearance. Similarly, ibuprofen (IV), choline magnesium trisalicylate, and salicylates (non-ASA) can increase penicillin G levels through plasma protein binding competition or reduced renal clearance. These interactions require careful monitoring. Certain antibiotics, such as doxycycline, minocycline, tetracycline, omadacycline, and sarecycline, can reduce the bactericidal effects of penicillin G aqueous due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. These combinations should be avoided or alternative drugs should be used. Tetracyclines, in particular, may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins, and therapeutic efficacy should be closely monitored if used concomitantly. Penicillin G aqueous can also decrease the effectiveness of oral contraceptives containing ethinyl estradiol or dienogest/estradiol valerate by altering intestinal flora, potentially leading to contraceptive failure. Additional or alternative forms of birth control may be advisable during concurrent use. Interactions with other drugs, such as probenecid, pretomanid, vadadustat, and fostemsavir, can increase penicillin G levels by inhibiting renal clearance or specific transporters like OATP1B1/3 or OAT3. These interactions may necessitate dose adjustments and close monitoring for adverse effects. Penicillin G aqueous can also reduce the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines, such as the cholera vaccine and typhoid vaccine (live), due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. These vaccines should not be administered to patients who have received systemic antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2–4 days before initiating microbiota oral therapy, as antibacterial agents may decrease the efficacy of bacterial spore-based treatments. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with penicillin G aqueous. These reactions are more likely in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs), such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), have also been reported. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if SCARs or allergic reactions occur, and alternative treatments should be considered. Prolonged or repeated use of penicillin G aqueous may lead to overgrowth of nonsusceptible organisms, including fungi, or secondary infections. Appropriate measures, such as incision and drainage or surgical procedures, should be taken in conjunction with antibiotic therapy if superinfections occur. Penicillin G aqueous should be administered with care to avoid intravascular or accidental intra-arterial injection, as well as injection near major peripheral nerves or blood vessels, to prevent neurovascular damage. Intravenous administration should be performed cautiously due to the risk of thrombophlebitis. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce treatment effectiveness and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance, rendering future treatments with penicillin G or other antibacterial drugs less effective. Dosage adjustments may be necessary in patients with renal or hepatic impairment based on the severity of the condition. Penicillin G aqueous is generally considered safe during pregnancy (Category B) and is excreted in breast milk. Its half-life ranges from 20–50 minutes (extended to 3–5 hours in end-stage renal disease), with peak plasma levels occurring at 30 minutes (IM) or 1 hour (IV). Approximately 65% of the drug is protein-bound, and it crosses the placenta but has poor diffusion across the blood-brain barrier. It is metabolized hepatically to active metabolites and excreted primarily in the urine. Penicillin G aqueous exerts its bactericidal activity by interfering with the synthesis of cell wall mucopeptides during active bacterial multiplication. It is compatible with certain additives and should be administered using appropriate infusion materials to avoid complications.
